The working waterfront: what the painters were looking at
The harbor in the paintings was a factory. This page explains what the painters were looking at — fish flakes, dories, schooners, nets — and where the working waterfront can still be seen.
Low wooden racks on which split, salted cod was laid out in the sun to dry. Whole fields of them appear in Lane’s and later paintings of the waterfront⟦0⟧.
Nets hung like a curtain in the water, catching fish by the gills. Mellen’s ⟦0⟧Gloucester Harbor (Laying Nets)⟦1⟧ shows crews setting them⟦2⟧.

Small flat-bottomed boats carried on the schooners and rowed out to set lines and nets; Gordon Parks photographed Gloucester crews laying nets by hand from them in 1943⟦0⟧. Homer drew boys in dories in 1873.
The fore-and-aft rigged vessels of the Gloucester fleet that brought fish home from the banks⟦0⟧.
Motor trawlers that drag a net along the bottom; Emile Gruppé painted them at the wharves.
A berth where a vessel is taken out of the water for repair. Hassam painted one in the 1890s.
Leonard Craske’s ⟦0⟧Man at the Wheel⟦1⟧, dedicated August 23, 1925⟦2⟧. The plaques list 5,368 men known to have been lost at sea; a single storm in 1862 took 120 men, and storms in 1879 took 159⟦3⟧.
At its peak Gorton’s ran dozens of wharves and many flake yards, where cod from the North Atlantic banks was split, salted and dried⟦0⟧.
The harbor’s museum of its own working history, on the inner harbor⟦0⟧.
The point where Lane painted Ten Pound Island (site 1) and Hopper painted the fishermen’s houses of the Italian Quarter⟦0⟧.
Rothko’s 1934 wharfs had fish flakes on the pier, the last generation of the racks Lane had painted eighty years before⟦0⟧.

The working harbor was photographed for the federal government twice: by Arthur Rothstein in 1937⟦0⟧ and by Gordon Parks, who went to sea on the ⟦1⟧Alden⟦2⟧ in 1943⟦3⟧. Those photographs are on ⟦4⟧the photographers page⟦5⟧.

Painting Cape Ann in winter: low light, sea smoke and the sun’s times
Most painters leave Cape Ann in October. They miss the year’s lowest, warmest light, the empty beaches and, on the coldest mornings, sea smoke over the harbor.
noon sun at the winter solstice, against 71° in June
of daylight on December 21, against 15 h 18 m in June
where the solstice sun sets (238°), far round to the left of the summer sunset
At midday in December the sun is about as high as it is at 5:55 p.m. in mid-July, so every hour of a winter day has the long shadows and raking light that summer painters wait for in the evening.
Height of the sun above the horizon at midday, on the 15th of each month. Winter months in ochre. Computed with the guide’s NOAA solar code for Gloucester Harbor.
The sun over Gloucester Harbor (42.61° N, 70.66° W). Times are local clock time.
The latest sunrise is about 7:13 a.m., in early January (around January 3). For any other day and place, use the sun planner on ⟦0⟧the chart⟦1⟧.

Sea smoke forms when very cold air moves over water that is much warmer than it, usually when the air is below about 10°F. The water evaporates and condenses at once into fog that rises in columns⟦0⟧. Look for it on the first still, clear morning after an Arctic cold front, just after sunrise, from Stacy Boulevard or the Rocky Neck causeway.

Lane painted the harbor frozen in the 1850s. Aldro Hibbard, who taught in Rockport, painted it under snow; the Museum of Fine Arts bought his ⟦0⟧Winter Days⟦1⟧ in 1920⟦2⟧, and the Smithsonian American Art Museum owns his ⟦3⟧Rockport Winter⟦4⟧⟦5⟧.
Oil paint keeps working in the cold; watercolor and acrylic freeze. If you use water media, work small and fast and keep the water in a vacuum flask.
Paint from the car on the worst days. Several historic views are close to public parking, among them Stacy Boulevard and Rocky Neck.
Fingerless gloves under mittens, two pairs of socks and a foam pad to stand on.
Ice makes the granite ledges and the Dog Bar Breakwater dangerous. Stay off them when they are wet or frozen.
The sun sets as early as 4:08 p.m. in early December (earliest around December 8). Plan to finish by about 3:30 p.m. and pack up in daylight.
Aaron Siskind’s Gloucester abstractions of 1944–45, Gordon Parks aboard the Alden in 1943 and Arthur Rothstein’s 1937 docks: where to see the photographs, with links to every collection.

Cape Ann was photographed by some of the century’s best: the government’s documentary photographers in the 1930s and 1940s, and Aaron Siskind, who found abstraction on its wharves. None of these photographs is reproduced here; each link goes to the museum or library that holds it.

Siskind came in July 1944 to a studio Adolph Gottlieb had found for him, and spent his mornings on the wharves and beaches with a camera and tripod. In Gloucester he turned from documentary work to close, flat views of peeling walls, rope, a discarded glove and granite. His painter friends Gottlieb, Barnett Newman and Mark Rothko encouraged him⟦0⟧. The curator Jan Howard called these summers his breakthrough⟦1⟧.
Try it⟦0⟧Paint as he looked: pick a square meter of a wharf wall, a stack of traps or a weathered door, and fill the whole picture with it.
1943, for the Office of War Information

Parks photographed Gloucester’s fishing families at home and went to sea with the crew of the ⟦0⟧Alden⟦1⟧, who laid their nets by hand from dories. The assignment was part of a wartime project on food production⟦2⟧. The photographs are in the Library of Congress.
1937, for the Farm Security Administration
Rothstein photographed the fishing boats and docks in the fall of 1937; prints are in the New York Public Library and the Library of Congress⟦0⟧.
Friedlander photographed the city in 1981; the Museum of Modern Art owns ⟦0⟧Gloucester, Massachusetts⟦1⟧ of that year⟦2⟧.
Chiarenza, later Siskind’s biographer, photographed in Gloucester as a young man; the Whitney owns his ⟦0⟧Gloucester Window, Sailing Ship⟦1⟧ of 1962⟦2⟧.

Short, sourced lives of the painters who worked in Gloucester and on Cape Ann, from Fitz Henry Lane and Mary Blood Mellen to Rothko and Nell Blaine, and the chains of teachers and friends that brought them.
The painters of Cape Ann: their lives here and who brought whom

Cape Ann’s painters arrived by invitation more often than by chance. A teacher brought his class, a friend found a cottage, an older painter asked two young ones to come for the summer. These are their lives on Cape Ann, and the chains that brought them.
Read each chain left to right: each painter brought, taught or welcomed the next. Names link to the profiles below.
Born in Gloucester; painted it 1840s–1865

Gloucester’s own painter learned his trade in the lithography shops before turning to oil, and came home to paint the harbor for two decades⟦0⟧. The Cape Ann Museum holds 40 of his paintings, his first known work (a watercolor of 1830), about 100 drawings and all three of his lithographed views of the town⟦1⟧. He worked from careful measured drawings, then painted several canvases from each; see site 4.
Working with Lane from the mid-1850s

Born in Vermont and schooled in watercolor at a girls’ academy, Mellen married a Universalist minister in 1840. When his brother took the Gloucester pulpit in 1855, she came into Lane’s orbit and was soon working beside him, free to copy his drawings and sometimes his canvases. One painting carries both signatures. The museum notes she is often called a “copyist”, and that Lane plainly respected her work⟦0⟧.

Hunt brought the French Barbizon painters’ ideas to Boston and taught John La Farge and both William and Henry James. His summer studio in Magnolia drew other artists to Cape Ann, and from 1868 he opened his classes to women, many from Boston’s leading families⟦0⟧.

Homer left the studio in Gloucester. In 1873 he painted outdoors and made himself a master of watercolor, almost to the exclusion of oil; in 1880 he boarded on Ten Pound Island in the middle of the harbor⟦0⟧. Both summers are on the guide’s map as sites 1 and 2.

In 1890 the Kentucky-born painter brought a summer class of students from Boston and the Cincinnati Academy, apparently the first large class of its kind in town, and he went on to paint about a hundred Gloucester pictures⟦0⟧. He drew others after him, among them Theodore Wendel, Joseph DeCamp, John W. Alexander and John Twachtman. He is said to have kept two studios, one for the morning light and one for the afternoon⟦1⟧.

Twachtman spent his last summers at the Harbor View Hotel in East Gloucester, painting the boats and wharves. His view of the hotel from the end of its pier was on his easel when he died there in August 1902⟦0⟧; Duveneck had been painting beside him only days before⟦1⟧. Through his pupil Leon Kroll, his influence reached Edward Hopper⟦2⟧.

Philadelphia’s great portraitist, and from 1895 to 1915 the first woman to teach at the Pennsylvania Academy, Beaux first came with her family in the mid-1880s and stayed at the Fairview Inn. Fame cost her privacy, so in 1903 she rented a cottage on Eastern Point and by 1906 had built Green Alley, her house and studio there. Her 1930 memoir, ⟦0⟧Background with Figures⟦1⟧, credits her family for planting what grew for her in Gloucester⟦2⟧.

Prendergast made more than 2,300 paintings and drawings, many of them New England beaches. In his Gloucester watercolors a loose pencil sketch guided rather than governed the brush: he changed his mind as he went, so that figures turned into rocks, and he sharpened edges with touches of pastel⟦0⟧.
1912; Folly Cove from the 1930s

Twachtman’s student at the Art Students League, Kroll found Cézanne in Paris and showed at the 1913 Armory Show⟦0⟧. He brought Edward Hopper to Gloucester in 1912⟦1⟧. From the 1930s he and his wife Genevieve summered at Folly Cove near Halibut Point, bought a house there in 1944, and counted Paul Manship, Walker Hancock and Virginia Lee Burton among their friends⟦2⟧. He also painted the Bass Rocks footbridge that Rothko later sketched⟦3⟧.

Hopper’s 1912 oils are solid and dark. In 1923 he courted Josephine Nivison here and, at her urging, took up watercolor; the next summer the newlyweds came back on an extended honeymoon, exploring by foot and streetcar⟦0⟧. By 1928 his Gloucester sales had bought him a car⟦1⟧. The ⟦2⟧Hopper trail⟦3⟧ finds twelve of his subjects.

After the 1913 Armory Show, the Ashcan painter went looking for new ground. His friend Charles Winter urged Gloucester, and from 1914 Sloan rented a little red cottage at the head of Rocky Neck for five summers. It filled with painters: Stuart Davis, Agnes Richmond, Charles and Alice Beach Winter, Paul Cornoyer, Paul Tietjens. The Cape Ann Museum owns eight of his Gloucester pictures⟦0⟧. The cottage still stands at 252 East Main Street⟦1⟧.

Sloan invited him in 1915, and Davis called Gloucester “the place I had been looking for”. He came back for many summers through 1934, drawn to the schooners and the clutter of the docks. In time he left the easel and canvases behind and went out with only a sketchbook and pen, and in Gloucester he began combining several views and moments in one picture, the Cubist idea that runs through his later work⟦0⟧.

In 1919 Demuth painted Gloucester’s masts, roofs and church towers outdoors, cutting them into the ruled, transparent planes that became Precisionism⟦0⟧. The RISD Museum’s ⟦1⟧Gloucester⟦2⟧ has released its image to the public domain⟦3⟧.

Hartley shunned the busy waterfront for Dogtown, the abandoned colonial settlement in the middle of Cape Ann, which he thought looked like a cross between Easter Island and Stonehenge. He wrote poems on the backs of some of the paintings⟦0⟧. In 1931 he boarded with the Wilkens family at 9 Rocky Neck Avenue, treating the summer as a warm-up for a Guggenheim-funded trip to Mexico⟦1⟧.
Summers from 1916 and 1919

Bernstein first came in 1916 on a friend’s advice. Meyerowitz, born in Russia, had paid for his training by singing in the Metropolitan Opera; the two met through the People’s Art Guild and married in 1919⟦0⟧. In the early 1920s Ellen Day Hale lent them a Folly Cove cottage, and Bernstein’s ⟦1⟧New England Ladies⟦2⟧ (1925) records an elderberry-wine party there, guest by guest⟦3⟧. Meyerowitz’s ⟦4⟧Gloucester Humoresque⟦5⟧ marks the founding in 1922 of the North Shore Arts Association, which juried its shows, and the Gloucester Society of Artists, which proudly did not⟦6⟧.
Most summers from 1920 to 1945

Avery’s first Gloucester pictures still owe something to Twachtman; over his Cape Ann summers the forms flattened and the color took over. He held to one rule: simplify anything, invent nothing. In 1932 he brought his young friends Gottlieb, Rothko and Barnett Newman⟦0⟧. The museum dates his first visit to 1920; the Rocky Neck Art Colony says 1921⟦1⟧.

In 1934 Rothko and his wife, Edith Sachar, reached Gloucester before the Gottliebs and took the Calder Street house the Gottliebs had wanted⟦0⟧. He painted the fish wharfs from Banner Hill, the bathers, and his friends at handball; the catalogue raisonné lists 38 Gloucester sheets⟦1⟧. In 1965 he gave the memorial address for Avery, calling him above all a great poet⟦2⟧. The ⟦3⟧Rothko trail⟦4⟧ has every sheet you can see.
Gruppé opened the Gloucester School of Art on Rocky Neck in 1929 and ran it for thirty years. His advice to students: think of a shape first, not of a horse or a tree or a boat⟦0⟧.
1943; Rocky Neck 1954 and 1958; East Gloucester 1974–1996

A Hans Hofmann student and a founder of New York’s Jane Street Gallery, Blaine first came in 1943 and rented Rocky Neck studios in 1954 and 1958. ⟦0⟧Time⟦1⟧ named her one of five leading women artists in America in 1957. Two years later polio left her in a wheelchair; she learned to paint again, and from 1974 summered at Eudora Cottage in East Gloucester, painting her garden, the ledges and the harbor⟦2⟧.
More lives are on the ⟦0⟧Women of Cape Ann trail⟦1⟧ (Martha Walter, Sally Michel Avery, Jane Peterson, Virginia Lee Burton) and the ⟦2⟧photographers page⟦3⟧.
